chunks.content: Strengths and limitations of this study A rigorous methodological framework was used. This scoping review identified the best clinical and organisational indicators for the optimal management of acute stroke, leading to improved oversight of quality of care. Indicator selection was conducted by a panel of interdisciplinary experts, including a patient partner, who assessed the indicators based on validity, relevance and measurement. Study selection and data extraction were carried out by two independent reviewers, on a 10% random sample of identified articles. Only French and English studies were included in the scoping review. Background Stroke is a leading cause of severe long-term disability. The incidence of stroke is increasing and affects over 13 million people worldwide each year, which demonstrates the necessity of interdisciplinary care and services for these hospitalised patients. During an ischaemic stroke, priority of treatment is based on methods to restore cerebral blood circulation as quickly as possible. Revascularisation treatments include intravenous thrombolysis, which breaks up clots obstructing the cerebral artery, or a thrombectomy, which removes a clot using endovascular techniques. Thrombectomy is another acknowledged and preferred practice for removing clots from large blood vessels since 2015. Furthermore, in 2016, a meta-analysis of these five randomised trials demonstrated significant benefits for most patients. However, this new treatment that is part of the stroke guidelines, is only offered in subspecialised centres staffed by neurointerventionists, providing a major impact on the reorganisation of care and services offered to the population to ensure accessibility. Additionally, evolving healthcare needs require healthcare systems to constantly adapt to meet demand, leading to major changes surrounding the governance of the healthcare system at provincial, national and international levels. Thus, the care and services provided following a revascularisation treatment must be consistent with the best practices. In addition, a study realised between 2010 and 2014 demonstrated that the reduction of care gaps in stroke quality indicators during hospitalisation improved the quality of life ≤180 days. It is therefore important to systematically assess the quality of stroke care in the acute stroke phase. The acute phase is the period during which the patient is hospitalised following an ischaemic stroke for which revascularisation treatment may have been administered. This phase begins as early as the first few hours when the patient is admitted to an acute care unit, and continues until the patient leaves the hospital after discharge. It generally includes early rehabilitation and the planning of the interventions with the interdisciplinary team in collaboration with the patient and family caregivers. It also involves referral to the care and services required according to the patient’s needs including referral to rehabilitation as well as secondary prevention. Regarding the acute phase, national and international guidelines in the scientific and grey literature recommend optimising practices and supporting hospital managers and clinicians. These recommendations are updated regularly to enable the design and implementation of a personalised action plan for stroke care in each organisation based on its mission. In short, they focus on different interdisciplinary approaches tailored to each individual patient and their care partners. Recommendations for the acute phase involve several interventions that include the assessment of physical, mental and cognitive health, patient management, caregiver support and monitoring the improvement or deterioration of cognitive, language and motor functioning. They also aim to promote recovery and shared decision-making, prevent potential complications and stroke recurrence. To facilitate the application of recommendations in clinical and organisational practice, several indicators have been developed and employed to monitor quality of care for patients who had a stroke. A quality indicator is any reliable and valid measure of a state of health, clinical practice or healthcare organisation. Numerous indicators developed by the expert authors of scientific and grey literature studies, including guidelines are based on the best evidence available as well as an interdisciplinary expert consensus obtained through a selection method, such as a Delphi process. Indeed, there are many quality indicators across the continuum of stroke care. Antecedent studies were mainly concerned with measuring indicators in terms of access to treatment and services in the hyperacute phase, including prehospital care, with an emphasis on time dependency. Specifically for the acute phase, in the last decade, there is no synthesis of indicators in the scientific and grey literature. Furthermore, these indicators have not been categorised with a view to assessing care performance based on accessibility of services, quality of care and resource optimisation as proposed by departments of health and social services. In light of these observations and despite a broad range of indicators for the acute phase, the manner in which these indicators have been validated and integrated into organisational and clinical practice remains unclear. To improve the clinical issues of patients who had a stroke, therefore, quality indicators must be rigorously selected to meet three criteria: relevance, validity and feasibility. This study aims to identify and synthesise evidence-based clinical and organisational quality indicators during the acute ischaemic stroke phase from 1 January 2015 until 28 February 2023. In this regard, the scoping review presented addresses the question: What evidence-based clinical and organisational quality indicators are conductive to the optimal interdisciplinary management of acute ischaemic stroke and are relevant, valid and feasible based on a consensus of experts? Method Study design and literature search strategies This scoping review is based on the six-step framework designed by Arksey and O’Malley (2005) and refined by Levac, Colquhoun and O’Brien (2010): (1) identification of research question, (2) identification of relevant studies using key words in different databases, (3) study selection, (4) data extraction, (5) data synthesis and (6) consultation with stakeholders. The detailed protocol of this scoping review ( ) is available on OSF Registries at https://osf.io/qc4mk/ . 10.1136/bmjopen-2023-073173.supp1 Supplementary data The search strategy included all empirical and theoretical writings relative to clinical and organisational quality indicators for the optimal interdisciplinary management and care of adults with acute ischaemic stroke. Four databases (MEDLINE, CINAHL, Academic search complete (EBSCO) and Cochrane Library) and search software (Google Scholar and Google) were consulted to identify relevant studies. An example of the search strategy with all databases is presented in . References of included studies were also screened for inclusion. The PICO mnemonic was used to highlight keywords related to the research question. The full detailed PICO mnemonic is presented in . The search involved combinations of the following terms: stroke quality indicators, adult patients who had an ischaemic stroke, acute phase (first few hours from the patient’s admission to an acute care unit until discharge from hospital), early inpatient rehabilitation (post-treatment, subacute or hospitalisation phase). Inclusion criteria referred to studies that included all types of clinical or professional interventions regarding stroke care in the acute phase as well as the development, implementation, assessment and comparison of quality indicators. Additionally, all scientific and grey literature studies done since 2015 in both English and French were included. Exclusion criteria referred to studies involving patients who had a haemorrhagic stroke or children. Studies that do not discuss quality indicators or that are conducted during pre-revascularisation, rehabilitation phase or post-rehabilitation phase including discharge home, long-term care, community-based rehabilitation and palliative care were excluded. 10.1136/bmjopen-2023-073173.supp2 Supplementary data 10.1136/bmjopen-2023-073173.supp3 Supplementary data Study selection and data extraction Study selection and data extraction were carried out by two independent reviewers (AB and TL) on a 10% random sample of identified articles to ensure accuracy using the Covidence software as recommended by and suggested by the Institut national d’excellence en santé et services sociaux in Quebec. Differences of opinion were debated, and a third reviewer (JH or LB) was contacted for further discussion until full consensus was reached. The extracted data included year of publication, city, publication status, authors, research design, study objective, the clinical and organisational quality indicators identified and authors’ categorisation of the indicators. The detailed data extraction is presented in . 10.1136/bmjopen-2023-073173.supp4 Supplementary data In order to properly measure concepts regarding the dimensions of healthcare performance, the indicators were attributed to a single category. Those measuring delays before receiving a service fell under ‘accessibility’ and those regarding access relative to geographical context and the concept of fair and equal access under ‘equity of access’. Indicators referring to hospital use rates or the proportion of patients to be hospitalised in a care unit were grouped under ‘efficiency’. Those that assess the protocols established to monitor patients or training offered or any other element implemented to ensure the good practice of long-term care were grouped under ‘viability’. Indicators assessing health outcomes, or the achievement of a care or service objective fell under ‘effectiveness’ and those measuring the coordination and integration of care under ‘continuity’. Finally, indicators measuring patients’ reaction or satisfaction or considering their needs for personalised care were grouped under ‘reactivity’. Identified and categorised clinical and organisational quality indicators were submitted to an advisory panel consisting of a neurologist, internist, nurse care manager, clinical consultant nurse specialist in neuroscience, patient partner, three registered nurses specialising in stroke care and four other health professionals working with patients who had a stroke (occupational therapist, physiotherapist, nutritionist and speech therapist). The members of the panel were chosen on the basis of their discipline, their centre, (primary, secondary and tertiary stroke centres) and their commitment to ischaemic stroke management. Their names and affiliations are listed in the acknowledgement section. This panel took part in an indicator selection process using a Delphi method. Panel members completed an online questionnaire to assess the relevance, validity and feasibility of measuring each indicator on a 5-point Likert scale with their opinions based on their expertise, respective points of view and personal clinical or organisational experience. Indicators with a result equal to or higher than 4 were retained and those with a result equal to or less than 3 were eliminated. The questionnaire has been validated by two content experts (JH and LB), a metrology expert (LB) and a scientific professional at the Institut national d’excellence en santé et services sociaux (INESSS) in Quebec. The statement for relevance was: « This indicator addresses an important problem and its use will lead to improved practice ». The statement for validity was: « This indicator is consistent with what it is intended to measure in practice ». Finally, the statement for feasibility was: « This indicator can be easily measured in practice based on the availability of data ». The level of concordance was the number of responses at 4 or 5 on the total numbers of responses per indicator. This equation was realised for every criteria (relevance, validity and feasibility). The scores were reported in percentage. Indicators with an agreement level equal or more than 60% were retained. The detailed results of the Delphi process are available in . 10.1136/bmjopen-2023-073173.supp5 Supplementary data Patient and public involvement A patient partner was included in the stroke expert panel for the selection of quality indicators. He has been recruited in keeping with the skills essential to this consultation: critical thinking, good judgement and the ability to express his position. This consultation ensured that the patient’s point of view was taken into account when evaluating quality indicators. Results A total of 4161 scientific publications and 182 literature publications were identified between 2015 and February 2023. After duplicates were removed, 3032 references were included in the screening strategy. After the titles were read, 2526 references were excluded mainly because the researchers did not focus on stroke care or had not been conducted during the acute post-stroke phase. Of these, 506 potentially relevant articles were assessed for eligibility based on inclusion and exclusion criteria with abstract or full text reading supported by Covidence software. Agreement between both reviewers (AB and TL) was over 90%. Ultimately, 31 articles were included in this scoping review because they contained quality indicators for the acute phase of ischaemic stroke. The identification and selection strategy is presented in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow chart in . General characteristics of included studies The majority of the 31 selected studies were conducted in Canada (22.6%), followed by Southeast Asia (19.4%), Australia (19.4%) and the USA (12.9%). Of those included, 15 were scientific and 16 were from the grey literature; the latter consisted, more specifically, of recommendations, guidelines or reports (51.6%). Eleven scientific studies concerned the evaluation of indicators using different methods (35.5%), two were systematic reviews with or without meta-analysis (6.4%) and one discussed a methodology for the development of indicators (3.2%). Characteristics of the included studies are presented in . Selection and synthesis of indicators Among the 31 selected studies, 364 indicators were identified. A total number of 119 indicators were subject to a preliminary screening by two stroke experts. Next, the 54 emergent indicators were reviewed by a panel of advisory stroke experts who assessed them using an online questionnaire. Finally, 34 indicators based on relevance, validity and feasibility were retained. The indicator selection process is presented in . These 34 indicators were then classified according to the eight dimensions of healthcare performance developed by the Quebec Ministry of Health and Social Services in Canada: accessibility, equity of access, safety, effectiveness, continuity, reactivity, efficiency and viability. The indicator with a high frequency of occurrence (12) was delay for the first rehabilitation assessment. Two indicators related to equity of access in terms of access relative to geographical context or fair and equal access. Five indicators were grouped under effectiveness to highlight resource optimisation and referred to rates of hospital use or proportion of patients hospitalised in a care unit and included the second indicator with the highest frequency of occurrence (15) that is the proportion of hospitalised patients treated in a stroke unit. There were no organisational indicators in relation to viability to assess the protocols established to monitor patient care or training offered or any other element implemented to ensure sustainability of good practice. Delay for the first rehabilitation assessment (accessibility), proportion of hospitalised patients treated in a stroke unit (effectiveness) and length of stay (effectiveness) were the organisational indicators with the highest frequency of occurrence. Of the clinical quality indicators, 12 related to safety and referred to the management of stroke risk factors and complications and included the indicator with the highest frequency of occurrence (19): dysphagia screening. Four indicators were grouped under effectiveness to assess health outcomes or achieve a care or service objective. Four indicators related to continuity to measure the coordination and integration of care. Finally, three indicators were grouped under reactivity to measure patient reaction or satisfaction or to consider their need for personalised care. Clinical indicators with the highest frequency of occurrence were: dysphagia screening (safety), antiplatelet therapy (safety) and prescription of an anticoagulant, lipid-lowering drugs, antiplatelet therapy, antihypertensive drugs or hypoglycaemic drugs on discharge (continuity). Discussion This scoping review aimed to identify clinical and organisational indicators in the acute stroke phase. Of the 31 studies selected, extraction of the indicators listed shows that some appeared more frequently than others in these articles. For each dimension, certain indicators were mentioned only once (eg, cardiac arrhythmia screening, percentage increase in telemedicine/telestroke coverage in remote communities ) or twice (eg, extracranial carotid artery assessment, secondary prevention programme referral on discharge). To our knowledge, no study has yet synthesised acute stroke phase indicators with a panel of experts to obtain a more accurate interdisciplinary assessment of the validity, relevance and feasibility of these indicators since the advent of thrombectomy. The methodology of most previous scoping reviews was based on the Arksey and O’Malley (2005) framework minus the sixth step regarding stakeholder consultation. Arksey and O’Malley maintain that the consultation stage is optional, but Levac, Colquhoun and O’Brien (2010) argue that this stage brings methodological rigour to the study and offers different perspectives regarding the results obtained. In the 31 selected studies, 16 references came from the grey literature whose authors had developed indicators from guidelines, recommendations and a literature review including an expert consensus. In fact, the development of key stroke indicators in 2021 in Canada had been done using a Delphi method allowing for a rigorous expert consensus that included a patient perspective. Our scoping review presents a broad range of indicators from an international literature review. However, the interdisciplinary expert panel consultation with a patient partner included in our study allowed us to highlight indicators that were relevant, valid and measurable in clinical and organisational practice from an interdisciplinary perspective. Furthermore, there were considerable differences in the way indicators were categorised in the studies included. In Canada, most of the guidelines classify indicators based on phases of the continuum of care for patients who had a stroke, namely, public awareness, stroke prevention, stroke care management (hyperacute, acute and rehabilitation phases) and reintegration into the community. In Quebec, recommendations also follow this trend. In a few other studies, indicators were classified according to Donabedian’s conceptual framework for assessing quality of care. This framework is classified according to three important and interdependent concepts: structure (attributes of the environment), process (acts and methods applied, as well as the organisation of care) and results (effects obtained in the provision of care, patient satisfaction and health status). The majority of these studies were process indicators and others were results indicators; there were no structural indicators. To obtain an overview of clinical and organisational practices for the acute stroke phase, however, selected indicators were categorised based on the dimensions of healthcare performance. Indeed, this performance framework can provide an overall picture of organisational and clinical practices while offering an essential interdisciplinary perspective and demonstrating a concern with the hospital context and the needs of patients who had a stroke. In fact, some of the indicators in our scoping review are outcome indicators (eg, modified Rankin Score, mortality, readmission), but are classified into the effectiveness indicators. Even if these indicators are not measured during the acute phase of ischaemic stroke, they are important to consider for optimal stroke recovery because care and services during this phase can impact health outcomes. As an example, a meta-analysis demonstrated that patients that are treated in a stroke unit reduces the number of complications and the mortality rate and improves functional independence. In fact, the large proportion of indicators categorised under safety seems to show that safety was a major health concern. The high risk of potential complications following a stroke or the recurrence of stroke may have contributed to an increase in this number of indicators. On the other hand, only two indicators were categorised under equity of access. Several previous studies demonstrate geographical inequalities, including in Canada, regarding the accessibility of revascularisation treatments for patients who had a stroke. In acute stroke care, there is a growing concern to provide equitable care for individuals experiencing ischaemic stroke in remote areas. Moreover, access to telehealth or telestroke should be offered to these patients to facilitate their access to organised stroke care across the continuum of care, including needs assessment and delivery of stroke rehabilitation care. Equitable access refers to the ability to provide care and services based on need and regardless of individual characteristics such as health, culture and sex and gender differences. Accordingly, more indicators are needed to measure this dimension of healthcare. Since only three indicators related to patients’ responsiveness, it appears that patients’ satisfaction and involvement in care is seldom measured in practice. Increasingly, studies show that patients must have a voice in their own care as well as in research and the development of guidelines. Finally, viability is not, apparently, measured in the acute stroke phase. If it were, it could determine how an organisation prepares for future breakthroughs, adapts to innovations and integrates these new elements into care, teaching and research planning. Some selected indicators were more prevalent than others, possibly owing to a certain variation in the criteria used when developing quality indicators. A systematic review reported that, in addition to validity, different criteria could influence the development of indicators; they include the cost of measurement promoting a prioritisation of indicators, stakeholder involvement in the development of indicators and transparency in the development process. Another study conducted in Australia in 2010 demonstrated a subset of indicators in stroke management that has been selected through value-based judgements by the National Advisory Committee given level of evidence, clinical relevance, consumer importance and ability for international comparisons. These authors assessed the statistical relationship between the process indicators and the clinical outcome, increasing the validity of the selected indicators. As well, there was variability in the definition, time and type of measurement between indicators. Most such differences could be attributed to the guidelines used (eg, delay for dysphagia screening within 4 hours, 24 hours or before oral intake). A scoping review was the preferred method for highlighting current and general knowledge relating to the clinical and organisational quality indicators essential for the optimal management of patients who had an acute stroke and their caregivers. This approach also made it possible to map the state of evidence-based knowledge, perform a critical analysis of the literature on the issue under study and paint a picture of the state of knowledge while meeting defined research objectives. This scoping review advanced knowledge regarding the indicators relevant for measuring the quality of acute stroke care, notably their synthesis and classification, based on dimensions of healthcare performance. It also served to supply needed information about how the indicators have been tested, validated and integrated in international organisations and clinical practice. The Registry of Stroke Care Quality is an initiative of the European Stroke Organisation which consists of a global data registry that focuses on improving care and services by regularly assessing quality and developing standards. Increasingly, studies are demonstrating the need for registries to help organisations measure indicators in clinical and organisational practice. The European Stroke Journal has published a methodology on how to develop a stroke quality registry, stroke management infrastructure and create education and training opportunities for healthcare professionals. Maintaining registries and making them accessible online is becoming increasingly popular and is something that will need to be factored into future research and continuous quality improvement plans for stroke care. This scoping review has certain limitations. First, this study was conducted only on ischaemic stroke. Second, it represents publications only from 2015, but this allows us to have up-to-date indicators that have been modified over the years to reflect the latest research findings. Third, it includes only articles in French and English, possibly excluding relevant articles published in other languages. Therefore, the selection criteria did not allow for the inclusion of many studies that would have been relevant, but subsequent addition of other studies did not allow for the addition of new emerging indicators. Fourth, results are applicable only to industrialised countries with a comparable healthcare system. Fifth, because resources were limited, independent verification of article selection and data extraction were done for only 10% of the total number of articles. Nevertheless, according to PRISMA-Scoping Review (ScR), when conducting a scoping review, duplicate selection and data extraction are optional. Despite these limitations, this study has several strengths. First, it highlights the organisational and clinical indicators that could optimise and improve the management of care and services during the acute phase in hospital for management of ischaemic stroke while taking into account certain long-term indicators that are highly relevant to the evaluation of patient health improvement. In fact, the expert panel consensus of interdisciplinary professionals including a patient partner significantly contributed to the assessment of the identified indicators in terms of quality criteria such as relevance, validity and feasibility. The panel of experts also helped to identify measurable indicators for hospitals with different missions as well as different geographical and structural contexts. A systematic review of all international stroke guideline registries revealed that few indicators in the registries represented their local priorities. Second, a rigorous methodological framework was used. Conclusion This scoping review is consistent with Canadian stroke guidelines and is also in line with the ministerial orientations of the Ministère de la Santé et des Services Sociaux of Quebec (MSSS), which aim to improve the performance of the healthcare system in terms of accessibility, care quality and resource optimisation. However, despite numerous quality indicators in the literature, the development and measurement of less explored dimensions of healthcare performance should be made. Finally, our scoping review supports a subsequent step involving the on-site evaluation of degree of success in achieving measurable, relevant and validated indicators impacting stroke management in the acute phase. Introduction A systematic study of the inpatient profile of patients and their diagnosis has seldom been made in the Indian context. Many neurological disorders like migraine, benign positional vertigo, cervical and lumbosacral radiculopathies, epilepsy, and neurodegenerative diseases like Parkinson’s disease are usually managed in an outpatient setting. Inpatient admissions for neurological disorders depend on various factors like the severity of the illness, the need for time-sensitive and expedited diagnosis and treatment, associated co-morbidities, the need for intravenous medical treatment, and other interventions. Patterns of admissions also vary depending on the regional prevalence of disorders and specialization of the treating centers. This study was done to understand the spectrum of diseases for which inpatient admissions were made to a tertiary center, so that the information acquired may help to streamline services, allocate appropriate resources, develop management protocols, design curricula, and improve training programs for postgraduate students. Materials and methods The study was conducted at a tertiary care neurological center in south India, with a large inpatient and outpatient burden. The neurological service at our center caters to 150 to 200 outpatients per day and 10 to 20 new inpatient admissions per day. The patients who had non-neurological diagnoses such as psychiatric disorders, systemic medical and rheumatological illnesses, and others who were transferred to units like neurosurgery were not included in this study. The final diagnosis was made after a detailed and thorough clinical evaluation by a team of four senior consultants, five junior consultants, three neuroradiologists, and six senior residents who were Doctor of Medicine (DM) trainees. All patients underwent comprehensive laboratory investigations, appropriate neuroimaging studies, and electrophysiological tests. The data obtained from the case records were entered into the Microsoft Excel database for descriptive analysis. Data entry was conducted confidentially, with exclusive access granted only to the consultants who utilized the central hospital inpatient database. Personal identifying information was deliberately masked. The data were securely stored on password-protected servers with restricted access limited to authorized personnel only. The collected data were part of ongoing registries on various neurological disorders that had prior Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals. Descriptive statistics including mean, standard deviation, and percentages were used to summarize the data. Results The overall study duration was 10 months, from January 2018 to October 2018. This period encompassed a three-month recruitment phase during which 1000 consecutive patients were enrolled. Subsequently, data entry and analysis were conducted over the remaining seven months. There were 606 males (60.6%) and 394 (39.4%) females. The average age of the patients was 48 years (±18.18). Three-hundred and seventy five (37.5%) patients were in the 40 to 60 age group, while 272 (27.2%) patients were in the 20-40 age group and 263 (26.3%) patients were in the 60-80 age group. There were 71 (7.1%) patients below 20 years and 19 (1.9%) patients above the age of 80 years. Strokes including arterial and venous strokes formed the major inpatient caseload, accounting for 48.7% (487/1000) of cases. Meningitis was diagnosed in 5.2% (52/1000) of patients; 4.8 % (48/1000) of patients had CNS demyelinating and autoimmune diseases. Ischemic strokes were the commonest accounting for 84% of strokes. Large artery atherosclerosis was the most common stroke sub-type followed by small vessel disease. In a study from south India, in 2642 patients with stroke, over 10 years, 78.4% had ischemic strokes and 21.6% had hemorrhagic strokes. Though headache is treated on an outpatient basis and is one of the most common diagnoses in OPD neurology clinics, [ ] migraine continues to be an important reason for inpatient admissions. Studies from Western countries like the USA have shown, 63% of admitted headaches were for treatment of migraine [ ]. Similarly, in a district general hospital in England, 17.7% of neurology admissions were for headaches [ ]. In India though, there are several studies of headache burden in the community and outpatient setting, a systematic study on the inpatient burden of headache is not found. There are few studies concerning the prevalence and spectrum of demyelinating disorders in India. In a study from South India, of 79 patients with demyelinating diseases, 35 had multiple sclerosis. In the area of teaching and examination, it is recommended that the curriculum should follow a pattern of “must know” subjects, which should constitute 70%, “important to know subjects” constituting 20%, and “good to know” subjects constituting 10%. These resources may include didactic lectures, case presentations, group discussions, journal clubs, workshops, and seminars. Conclusions The most common five neurological disorders for which patients were admitted were stroke, seizure, headache, meningitis, and autoimmune/demyelinating disorders. These five disorders should be given priority in resource allocation, teaching curricula, training programs, and neurology examinations. This will enable us to have standardized protocols and streamline neurological care across the country. This will also empower qualifying postgraduates to manage the common neurological disorders prevalent in the population confidently and effectively.

chunks.content: Introduction Worldwide, stroke was the third leading cause of mortality in 2021, accounting for around 7 million deaths. The number of hospital admissions each year due to stroke is rising, and the age of presentation is falling, with a significant increase in cases under the age of 50 years noted. , , The majority of strokes are ischaemic in nature (approximately 65.3% globally as of 2025), and their rate is higher in higher-income countries, for example the USA where prevalence was 87%. , These are mostly caused by atherosclerosis and cardioembolic events, with the rising incidence attributable to an ageing population and increasing rates of cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes and obesity. Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is not an uncommon complication of stroke. However, guidelines regarding the use of thromboprophylaxis in this situation are not well defined. In this review, we consider the epidemiology of VTE post-stroke, the evidence for VTE prophylaxis and guideline recommendations, and provide practical suggestions for clinicians treating these patients. Methods PubMed and Google Scholar were utilised to identify relevant articles concerning the pathophysiology and incidence of VTE post-ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke, and evidence supporting VTE prophylaxis post-stroke (randomised controlled trials and meta-analyses). The current American, British, Canadian and European guidelines on VTE prophylaxis were gathered from the respective national guidelines. VTE post-ischaemic stroke VTE is a common complication of ischaemic stroke. The risk of VTE may be up to 20-fold higher, compared to an age-matched healthy population during the initial month following an ischaemic stroke (HR 19.7, 95% CI 10.1–38.5), up to 10-fold higher during the first 3 months post-stroke (HR 10.6, 95% CI 5–22.5), and two-fold higher for the first year (RR 2.19, 95% CI 1.85–2.60). , , A Norwegian study found the incidence of stroke in the general population to be 1.43 per 1,000 (CI 1.33–1.54). Without the use of heparin prophylaxis, the incidence of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), usually asymptomatic, below-knee DVT, is around 50% in the first 2 weeks following an acute stroke, with a peak incidence during days 2–7. , This risk persists into the rehabilitation phase, with DVT rates of one-third reported in patients admitted to a rehabilitation unit, on average 9 weeks post-stroke. The main risk posed by an asymptomatic DVT is that of a subsequent pulmonary embolism (PE). PEs tend to present after the first week of stroke and have been shown to contribute to 7–30% of mortality post-stroke. , , Non-fatal PEs can also cause significant morbidity, impacting on cardiorespiratory reserve and quality of life. Virchow’s triad, comprising damage to blood vessel endothelium, circulatory stasis and a hypercoagulable state, forms the foundation of thrombus formation in VTE. Risks for VTE post-stroke include immobilisation, infection, presence of indwelling lines, cancer, obesity, stroke severity, length of hospital stay and the requirement for rehabilitation, which all impact on Virchow’s triad. , , In addition, ischaemic stroke is a thrombo-inflammatory condition, characterised by platelet activation, oxidative stress and the presence of increased numbers of proinflammatory neutrophils and neutrophil extracellular traps, which may further promote VTE. , Haemorrhagic transformation of ischaemic stroke Haemorrhagic transformation (HT) following acute ischaemic stroke occurs due to disruption of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) and reperfusion injury. , Acute HT occurs within 18 h of stroke onset, and delayed HT occurs after 18 h. Matrix-metalloproteinases (MMP), in particular MMP-9, play a key role in the development of HT. In the acute phase, this is mostly released from activated neutrophils in the peripheral blood, whereas in delayed HT, it is primarily sourced from microglia and astrocytes. , An increased neutrophil:lymphocyte ratio was shown to be associated with risk of HT in over 1,000 patients with acute ischaemic stroke. Fibrinolysis initiated by exogenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) causes a consumptive coagulopathy, with prolongation of the prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, which may last more than 24 h post-infusion. , , This coagulopathy is driven primarily by marked reductions in fibrinogen levels, which correspond with the risk of subsequent HT and parenchymal haematoma formation. Alongside causing clot lysis, tPA promotes MMP-9 release from neutrophils and activates an agonist of platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha, which further promotes disruption of the BBB. , A meta-analysis of all completed phase 3 randomised controlled trials of alteplase reported HT in 6.8% of alteplase-treated participants, with an OR of 5.55 (95% CI 4.01–7.7) compared with placebo. Overall, rates of intracranial haemorrhage (ICH) related to thrombolysis use have been reported at 2–7% in post-marketing evaluation. , Antiplatelet therapy may potentially further increase the risk of HT. Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) is recommended for patients following a minor stroke or high-risk transient ischaemic attack (TIA) with only a minor impact on the risk of ICH noted in clinical trials, compared with aspirin monotherapy (rates of HT <0.5% for monotherapy or DAPT with aspirin and clopidogrel

Development of VTE post-ICH Worryingly, VTE is more prevalent following ICH than ischaemic stroke. Risk of DVT is approximately four times greater, with in-hospital VTE rates of 1–7% reported, the majority of which occur within the first week after presentation. , , , Severity of haemorrhage, age, prolonged hospitalisation, functional impairment post-stroke (especially immobility) and comorbidities such as the presence of cancer, pulmonary circulation disease, infection and coagulopathy have been identified as risk factors for VTE post-ICH. , , A number of authors have created risk prediction models for in-hospital DVT, although none have reached clinical practice. , One group created a nomogram to predict VTE based on only three variables: NIHSS score at presentation, Glasgow coma scale score on admission and D -dimer level. A simple tool to identify high-risk patients is attractive; however, this score was derived from a reasonably modest sample size of 369 patients, with a high rate of VTE (22.5%) observed, and limited information provided regarding implementation of thromboprophylaxis. Another group produced a risk assessment model based on age, haematoma volume, presence of extension into the subarachnoid space, pneumonia, gastrointestinal bleeding and length of stay, termed the ICH-VTE score. This was derived from a cohort of over 1,300 patients and validated in nearly 1,000 more. However, whether higher-risk patients benefit from a different management strategy is not known. The size of the haematoma itself is capable of causing secondary brain injury, which would warrant an inflammatory response. The complement cascade is activated as inflammatory markers are raised, increasing the patient’s risk of developing a clot. Another factor contributing to this inflammation is raised intracranial pressure and midline shift. In response to the bleed, the immune system tries to compensate by releasing inflammatory cytokines (IL-6 and TNF-α), which propagate the production and release of fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor from the liver. VTE prophylaxis after ischaemic stroke Non‐pharmacological prophylaxis Intermitted pneumatic compression stockings (IPCs) have been identified as a means of reducing the risk of DVT in hospitalised surgical patients. A meta-analysis that analysed over 16,000 patients from 70 RCTs reported a rate of 7.3% in patients wearing IPCs versus 16.7% in those with no intervention (p < 0.001). To investigate whether this is applicable to hospitalised stroke patients, another study examined graduated compression stockings (GCS) and IPCs in 2,615 and 177 acute ischaemic stroke patients respectively. Although IPCs did not have a significantly improved outcome, there was a trend in reduction of DVTs versus control groups of providing ‘best medical intervention only’ (OR 0.45, CI 0.37–2.89). The Clots in Legs Or sTockings after Stroke (CLOTS3) Trials reviewed 2,876 patients across 76 centres in the UK, reporting an absolute risk reduction of DVT by 3.6% associated with use of IPCs. Out of 1,438 control patients 12.1% had a DVT, whereas in those given IPCs the rate was 8.5% (CI 1.4–5.8). IPCs have also been identified as a valuable method for prophylaxis when pharmacological intervention is contraindicated; however, complications of these devices include skin irritation, puritus and, rarely, tissue damage and infection, which may limit their value. Another non-pharmacological intervention is the geko™ electronic stimulation device. This device sits below the knee and stimulates the common peroneal nerve to contract the calf muscle, providing an imitation of walking. By increasing venous return and reducing stasis, the geko™ device is able to improve circulation and theoretically prevent clots from forming. The geko™ was utilised in six stroke patients, with DVT rates compared to 35 controls allocated IPCs. The rate of DVT was lower in the group receiving the novel device (22.9% versus 50%) in this small audit report. This device may be more tolerable from a patient perspective than IPCs, but larger well-designed clinical studies are required to determine its role in clinical practice. Pharmacological prophylaxis The value of pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis in hospital inpatients is essentially universally accepted. However, although there is clearly a high risk of VTE following a stroke, the data supporting the routine use of VTE prophylaxis in these patients are less clear. The International Stroke Trial (IST) randomised 19,435 patients post-ischaemic stroke to up to 14 days of unfractionated heparin (UFH) (5,000 or 12,000 IU twice daily) compared with ‘no heparin’. PEs occurred in 0.5% of the heparin arm and 0.8% of the no heparin arm within 14 days, whereas HT was more common in patients receiving anticoagulation (1.2% vs. 0.4%). 312 patients were randomised to high-dose nadroparin (4,100 IU twice daily), low-dose nadroparin (4,100 IU once daily) or placebo for 10 days, with the first dose received within 48 h of presentation. HT on routine CT scan at day 10 was present in 6.2%, 8.6% and 12% of patients receiving high-dose LMWH, low-dose LMWH or placebo respectively. No patients receiving LMWH developed a DVT, versus one patient in the placebo arm. The PROTECT (prophylaxis of thrombotic and embolic events in acute ischaemic stroke with the LMWH certoparin) trial randomised 545 patients within 24 h of stroke onset to certoparin (3,000 IU once daily) or UFH (5,000 IU three times daily) for 12–16 days. The primary endpoint of proximal DVT, PE or death due to VTE occurred in 6.6% and 8.8% of the LMWH and UFH arms, respectively, and similarly proximal DVT occurred in 6.6% and 8.4%. The trial concluded that certoparin was non-inferior to UFH. The PREVAIL (efficacy and safety of enoxaparin versus UFH for the prevention of VTE after acute ischaemic stroke) study randomised 1,762 patients with acute ischaemic stroke within 48 h of symptom onset to 40 mg enoxaparin once daily or 5,000 IU UFH twice daily for 10 days. Significantly more patients in the UFH arm developed VTE (18% vs. 10%, p = 0.0001), which was primarily driven by an increased rate of asymptomatic DVT (17% vs. 10%, p < 0.0001). ICH occurred in 1% in both arms, and bleeding rates overall were similar. A number of meta-analyses have been published in this area. Analysis of eight randomised trials (15,405 patients), comparing heparin prophylaxis with no heparin, reported an increase in major bleeding events (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.20–2.28), but no impact on death or rates of PE. A more recent Cochrane review of nine RCTs (3,137 patients) comparing LMWH with UFH demonstrated a reduction in DVT risk in the LMWH group (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.44–0.70) but no difference in risk of DVT, HT or mortality rate. These data, while useful, have significant limitations. Patients with a history of ICH, uncontrolled hypertension, or severe stroke-related morbidity were excluded from the majority of randomised studies, hence generalisability is compromised. It is also not clear when the appropriate time to start VTE prophylaxis in all patients is, nor how long this should be continued for. Factor Xa inhibitors have not been trialled specifically in the stroke population, but provide an attractive oral option for longer-term prophylaxis than subcutaneous injections. The MARINER (Medically Ill Patient Assessment of Rivaroxaban Versus Placebo in Reducing Post‐Discharge Venous Thrombo‐Embolism Risk) and MAGELLAN (Multicentre, randomised, parallel‐group efficacy and safety study for the prevention of venous thromboembolism in hospitalised medically ill patients comparing rivaroxaban with enoxaparin) studies reviewed the use of low-dose rivaroxaban (10 mg once daily) for 25–45 days after hospitalisation. , A composite outcome of symptomatic DVT, non-fatal PE, myocardial infarction and ischaemic stroke occurred in 1.8% of rivaroxaban-treated patients compared with 2.31% of the placebo cohort. Approximately 16% of each arm were in hospital due to an ischaemic stroke; however, no subgroup analysis has been provided. One group randomised 75 patients to enoxaparin (40 mg once daily) versus compression stockings from 48 h after presentation. There was no evidence of haematoma enlargement at 72 h,7 days and 3 weeks in either group. Patients had planned doppler ultrasound and CT pulmonary angiography after 1 week. There were three asymptomatic DVTs in the LMWH group and one in the control arm, as well as one asymptomatic PE in either arm. One patient not allocated to LMWH sustained a symptomatic PE on day 17. The PREVENTIHS study (prevention of VTE in haemorrhagic stroke patients) was a phase 3 RCT comparing 40 mg enoxaparin once daily for 10 days versus placebo. Patients were enrolled 72 h after ICH, provided that a CT did not show further bleeding at that timeframe, and underwent Doppler ultrasonography after 10 days. DVT was detected in 16% of the LMWH group and 20% of the control group (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.29–2.12), which was not statistically significant; however, the study was terminated early with only 73 patients enrolled due to poor recruitment. Meta-analyses have also provided equivocal results. Review of four studies of 1,000 patients, in which heparin prophylaxis was commenced between 24 h and 6 days post-ICH, identified a significant reduction in PEs (1.7% vs. 2.9%, RR 0.37; 95% CI 0.17–0.8) in favour of VTE prophylaxis, and a non-significant reduction in mortality but increase in haematoma enlargement. A more recent analysis of nine studies including those in the previous meta-analysis (n = 4,055), in which prophylactic heparin was implemented from 24 h to 7 days post-presentation, also showed no significant impact on haematoma extension, mortality or extracranial bleeding. In terms of the optimal time to commence VTE prophylaxis, one group allocated 126 patients to early (within 48 h) or late (after 48 h) LMWH prophylaxis, with no difference in haematoma expansion reported. Another recent study compared enoxaparin (20 mg twice daily) given 24 (early) or 72 (late) hours after ICH in 139 patients, excluding those requiring neurosurgery. Patients underwent CT brain and Doppler ultrasound prior to discharge or as clinically indicated. Two patients in the early group and one in the late group developed DVT. Haematoma enlargement occurred in eight patients in each arm. Guideline recommendations Several guidelines make weak recommendations to consider VTE prophylaxis after 24–48 h in the absence of continued bleeding. These are summarised in ; , , , , however, real-world practice differs significantly. Of 32,690 patients with ICH who survived to day 2 of hospitalisation, only 16.5% received any anticoagulation, and in a survey of UK stroke clinicians, 28% felt that anticoagulation should not be used at all, which rose to 38% for patients after a lobar bleed, likely due to concerns regarding re-bleeding from possible CAA. A summary of available guideline recommendations is provided in . Where available, these essentially suggest commencing VTE prophylaxis 24–48 h post-ICH if feasible. Of note, no single guideline discusses both ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke management. Relevant interventional trials are summarised in . , , , , , , , , Conclusion Mortality due to stroke and its complications has become a growing concern in the developed world. Of the multiple complications a patient can develop, VTE is one of the more common ones, with a mortality rate of up to 30%. The development of VTE appears to rely heavily on venous stasis, endothelial dysfunction and a thromboinflammatory state in both ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke, with the highest risk of VTE occurring within the first 2 weeks. chunks.content: Plain language summary Intracranial aneurysms are abnormal outpouchings in the walls of intracranial arteries. They are present in approximately 3% of adults and are more common in women than in men. If an aneurysm ruptures, it causes a bleeding into the space between the brain and its surrounding membranes, known as aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. This type of stroke often occurs at a relatively young age: about half of affected patients are under 50 years old, and roughly two-thirds are women. Outcomes after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage are often poor. Approximately 40% of the patients die within 3 months, and among those who survive long term, outcomes vary widely. Roughly one-third of all patients regain independence in daily activities, while another group survives with some level of disability. Among survivors, cognitive and emotional problems are very common, including memory impairment, reduced concentration, fatigue and depression. Most survivors do not return to their pre-haemorrhage level of functioning. How well someone recovers after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage depends on how severe the bleeding is and on complications that may happen especially in the first 2 weeks after the bleeding. The most feared complications are rebleeding of the ruptured aneurysm (occurring in approximately 40% of the patients if the ruptured aneurysm remains untreated), reduced blood flow to the brain (which can cause symptoms in approximately 20% of patients) and a build-up of fluid in the brain (in approximately 25% of patients). Hospital care is mainly focused on preventing these complications, finding them early if they occur, and treating them. The ultimate goal is to improve recovery and long-term physical, cognitive and emotional functioning. This guideline provides recommendations based on high-quality studies from the medical literature, and opinions from experts if high-quality studies are lacking. The recommendations and expert opinions address when an aneurysm should be treated, which aneurysm treatment methods are best, and which drugs can help lower the risk of complications during hospital care. It also describes diagnostic methods that help physicians identify the cause of clinical deterioration and outlines the management of complications. In addition, it gives guidance on the appropriate hospital and specialist setting, taking into account patient volume and experience and on the timing of follow-up brain scans after aneurysm treatment. Based on a high level of scientific evidence, this guideline recommends that patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage should not receive antifibrinolytic drugs to reduce the risk of rebleeding, as they do not decrease the risk of poor outcome. In patients who are awake or only mildly drowsy, with at most mild neurological deficits, coiling without adjunctive devices is preferred over microsurgical clipping to treat the ruptured aneurysm in situations where both treatment options are equally suitable. All patients should receive oral nimodipine, a drug that reduces the risk of brain damage, but not other drugs such as statins, magnesium sulphate or endothelin receptor antagonists. Based on the opinion from experts, this guideline suggests that lowering blood pressure before the aneurysm is treated may help reduce the risk of rebleeding of the aneurysm in patients with very high blood pressure, but it remains unclear whether or not it decreases the risk of poor outcome. Blood pressure lowering should be performed slowly and in a controlled manner, ie, without undershoot, and with short-acting medications. The ruptured aneurysm should ideally be treated within 24 h, when possible, and by an experienced physician who treats at least 30 intracranial aneurysms (either ruptured or unruptured) per year. Treatment decisions should always be made by a multidisciplinary team (composed of at least 1 neurosurgeon and 1 neurointerventionalist) to consider the different aneurysm treatment options, and decide on the safest method, and the most effective and durable treatment outcome. For aneurysms that cannot be treated by regular coiling, ie, without adjunctive devices, there are no high-quality data showing that more novel endovascular techniques and devices (such as stent-assisted coiling, flow diverting stents or intra-saccular devices) decrease the risk of poor outcome compared to regular coiling. If a patient worsens due to reduced blood flow in the brain, raising blood pressure may be considered, but only after the aneurysm is secured and fluid administration has failed. Endovascular drug treatments may be used in patients with a critically reduced blood flow to the brain due to severe narrowing of the brain arteries, but treatments that widen the arteries by the use of inflatable balloons should only be considered as a last-line rescue treatment after careful multidisciplinary discussion of the potential risks and uncertain benefits. The current data are insufficient to support the use of temporary stents. Brain scans (CT and CT-perfusion) are useful when a patient’s condition worsens or cannot be assessed clinically. Routine invasive brain monitoring, EEG and complex monitoring systems are not recommended because benefits are unclear. If fluid builds up in the brain (hydrocephalus), drainage is recommended

Patients should be treated in a specialised neuro-ICU in centres that treat at least 70 patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage per year, or at least 35 in remote areas. After hospital discharge, follow-up brain scans can be made to investigate whether or not reopening of the aneurysm occurs after treatment. Follow-up imaging is only indicated as long as re-treatment of the aneurysm remains an option, and in the following situations that depend on type of aneurysm treatment: Patients treated with coils should have follow-up imaging at least once at or after 12 months after aneurysm treatment. Patients treated with clips usually do not need long-term follow-up imaging if imaging within 6 months after treatment shows that the aneurysm is completely occluded. Patients with partially occluded aneurysms or those who are treated with newer devices, such as intrasaccular devices or flow-diverting stents, need long-term follow-up. Patients who are at high risk of developing new aneurysms, such as those with a young age, positive family history for aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage or autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, should have scans every 5 years to check for new aneurysms. The median age of patients with aSAH is 52 years and most patients are women. Although the global incidence of aSAH has declined from 10.2 (95% CI, 8.4–12.5) per 100,000 person-years in 1980 to 6.1 (95% CI, 4.9–7.5) in 2010, the overall disease burden remains substantial, in part because of the relatively young age of affected patients. Subarachnoid haemorrhage resulted in approximately 350,000 deaths and more than 10 million disability-adjusted life years globally in 2021. The most important determinants of poor functional outcome after aSAH are the effects of the initial bleeding, rebleeding of the ruptured aneurysm, delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) and hydrocephalus. During hospitalisation, the management of patients with aSAH is focused on the prevention and treatment of complications resulting from aSAH to reduce the risk of death, disability and cognitive and emotional consequences. Since the publication of the European Stroke Organisation (ESO) guidelines for the management of intracranial aneurysms and subarachnoid haemorrhage in 2013, new data have been reported regarding the diagnosis, prevention and treatment of aSAH-related complications and radiological follow-up of treated aneurysms. These include, with varying levels of evidence, the use of antifibrinolytic drugs, novel treatment options for treatment of the ruptured aneurysm, use of lumbar drains and endovascular treatment of vasospasm. The aim of this guideline is to provide contemporary evidence-based recommendations and expert-consensus statements to guide neurosurgeons, neurologists, neurointensivists and (interventional) radiologists in the clinical management of patients with aSAH at the emergency room, during hospital admission and during follow-up, to reduce the risk of case-fatality and long-term disability. Where feasible, we conducted fixed-effects meta-analyses, estimating heterogeneity using the REML method, provided no substantial heterogeneity was detected. Expert consensus statements were modified using the Delphi method until consensus was reached regarding the phrasing of the statement. The expert consensus statements were then sent to all MWG-members for anonymous voting. Medical (non-)invasive treatment to decrease the risk of rebleeding and poor functional outcome PICO 1a In adult patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (aSAH), does treatment with antifibrinolytic drugs compared to no antifibrinolytic drugs decrease the risk of poor functional outcome? Analysis of current evidence We identified 12 RCTs comparing treatment with antifibrinolytic drugs vs no antifibrinolytic drugs, and 1 recent Cochrane review. Eleven RCTs studied the effect of tranexamic acid, and 1 trial the effect of epsilon amino-caproic acid on aneurysm rebleeding or functional outcome. Ten RCTs were performed in an era during which aneurysm treatment was postponed to the post-delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) period. In those trials, the effect of long-term treatment with antifibrinolytic drugs was studied. The 2 most recent RCTs studied the effect of short-term treatment. , The largest RCT also included patients with non-aneurysmal SAH. From that trial, we extracted data on patients with aneurysmal SAH. Pooled analyses of all available RCTs showed that treatment with antifibrinolytic drugs does not decrease the risk of poor functional outcome (odds ratio [OR]: 1.03; 95 CI, 0.86–1.23; ) or case-fatality (OR: 0.96; 95% CI, 0.81–1.15; ), despite a decreased risk of rebleeding (risk ratio [RR]: 0.56; 95% CI, 0.37–0.83; ). The discrepancy between a reduced risk of rebleeding and a neutral effect on outcome has been explained as resulting from a higher risk of ischaemic complications and hydrocephalus in patients treated with antifibrinolytic drugs, or impeded recovery from ischaemic injury. The 2 most recent RCTs were performed in an era that reflects current clinical practice with early aneurysm treatment and both microsurgical and endovascular aneurysm treatment options. , Only the Ultra-early tranexamic acid after subarachnoid haemorrhage (ULTRA) trial was adequately powered to detect a potential effect on clinical outcome. In ULTRA, tranexamic acid was started in the initial hospital directly after head CT confirmed a diagnosis of SAH. The median time between ictus and CT diagnosis was 93 min, and the time between ictus and the start of tranexamic acid was 185 min. Treatment of the ruptured aneurysm occurred after a median time of 14 h after CT diagnosis. In the 955 participants with SAH, tranexamic acid had no statistically significant effect on rebleeding (OR: 0.71; 95% CI, 0.48–1.04) and did not decrease the odds of poor functional outcome (OR: 1.16; 95% CI, 0.89–1.50) or case-fatality (OR: 1.15; 95% CI, 0.86–1.54) in the whole study population. Similar results were found in the subgroup of 813 patients with aneurysmal SAH. Although a statistically significant reduction in rebleeding was observed (OR: 0.66; 95% CI, 0.44–0.99), no effect on poor functional outcome (OR: 1.08; 95% CI, 0.82–1.43) or case-fatality (OR: 1.11; 95% CI, 0.82–1.51) was found. Short-term treatment with tranexamic acid did not increase the risk of DCI (OR: 0.99; 95% CI, 0.72–1.36) or hydrocephalus (OR: 1.23; 95% CI, 0.93–1.63). In conclusion, the ULTRA trial provided strong evidence that very early and very short-lasting antifibrinolytic therapy does not decrease the risk of poor functional outcome in patients with aSAH. Additional information After publication of the ULTRA trial, several studies were performed to investigate the effect of tranexamic acid in certain subgroups. Patients with a good clinical condition on admission and men treated with tranexamic acid had worse functional outcomes compared to those not treated with tranexamic acid. No effect on outcome was observed in patients with a poor clinical condition on admission and in women. Although the start of tranexamic acid > 6 h after ictus was associated with a reduced risk of rebleeding, it did not result in better outcomes. Analysis of current evidence We did not identify any RCTs during the last 4 decades investigating the effect of antihypertensive drugs with the primary aim of decreasing the risk of rebleeding of the ruptured aneurysm and thereby improving outcome. Additional information Several observational studies investigated the relationship between antihypertensive drug treatment and the risk of rebleeding. One study showed that blood pressure treatment may decrease the risk of rebleeding, but not poor outcome, potentially as a result of an increased risk of cerebral infarction. A study without a control group found that the incidence of rebleeding was low (3.1%) after the implementation of a strategy of intensive systolic blood pressure reduction (target 120 ± 20 mm Hg). Another study found that after the implementation of a blood pressure management protocol (systolic blood pressure target of 160 mm Hg), the incidence of in-hospital rebleeding declined from 6.7% to 2.8% (OR: 0.4; 95% CI, 0.10–1.63) and the incidence of DCI from 44.2% to 7.7% (OR: 0.10; 95% CI, 0.04–0.23). A recent study compared the incidence of in-hospital rebleeding between a hospital with a policy of aggressive blood pressure lowering (systolic blood pressure target before aneurysm treatment ≤ 140 mm Hg) vs a hospital with a more liberal blood pressure approach, and found a trend (adjusted HR 0.66 [95% CI, 0.23–1.92]) towards a lower incidence of rebleeding in the hospital with a more aggressive blood pressure lowering strategy. However, there were differences in risk factors for rebleeding between the 2 centres, which introduced major bias. PICO 2 In adult patients with aSAH, does early aneurysm occlusion compared to no early aneurysm occlusion decrease the risk of poor functional outcome? Analysis of current evidence We identified only one small RCT that assessed the timing of aneurysm treatment. The study was conducted in the pre-coiling era and included 211 good-grade (Hunt and Hess grades I–III) aSAH patients (aged 16 to 65 years) admitted to a single hospital between 1985 and 1987. Patients with intracerebral haematomas, decreased level of consciousness or severe neurological deficits were excluded. All included patients had anterior circulation aneurysms, and patients were randomly assigned to early (0–3 days), intermediate (4–7 days) or late (8 days and later) surgical clipping. Sixteen patients never underwent aneurysm surgery due to severe deterioration or death before the planned surgery. Delayed cerebral ischaemia and rebleeding were the main causes of preoperative deterioration. None of the patients received antifibrinolytic agents or hypertensive drug treatment, while intramuscular betamethasone 4 mg 4 times daily was routinely given. Of the 211 patients, 159 randomly received either intravenous followed by oral nimodipine or placebo treatment up to 21 days. The 3-month case-fatality rates were not different between early, intermediate and late surgery groups (case-fatality rates of 6%, 6% and 13%, respectively). Using a 3-point outcome scale (independent, dependent, death), 92% of the early surgery group patients were independent at 3 months, 79% in the intermediate group and 80% in the late surgery group. However, dependency was significantly higher in the intermediate surgery group (11 patients, 16%) in comparison to the early surgery group (2 patients, 3%). In summary, early surgery within 3 days after bleeding in comparison to delayed surgery did not lead to higher case-fatality. A comparison between early and intermediate surgery groups (late surgery group excluded) suggested that 3-month functional outcome was better for patients operated early. During the endovascular treatment era (since the early 1990s), no randomised trial has addressed the effect of timing of aneurysm occlusion on outcome of SAH patients. Additional information Due to the paucity of high-quality studies, recent (published within the last 10 years) meta-analyses were reviewed as supporting information. These meta-analyses generally include lower quality studies, which have inherent selection and treatment biases. In a meta-analysis including 16 observational studies of endovascular aneurysm occlusion, treatment within 24 h reduced the odds for poor outcome in comparison to patients treated at > 1 day, but not when compared to 24–72 h. Another meta-analysis of surgical patients included the only published randomised trial, 1 prospective and 12 retrospective studies for quantitative analyses. Early surgery, defined as surgery within 3 days, was associated with better outcomes irrespective of the clinical condition on admission and a higher survival rate. Similarly, in a third meta-analysis published in 2017, aneurysm treatment within 48 h was compared to treatment between 48 h and 7 days, and to delayed (>7 days) treatment of poor-grade SAH patients. The meta-analysis included all published studies (even small case series) between 1990 and 2014 that reported on surgical or endovascular treatment for poor-grade SAH patients. A total of 26 studies with 1255 patients assessed outcomes by treatment timing. Based on these highly miscellaneous data, the authors concluded that poor-grade SAH patients treated within 48 h had the highest rates of

on admission and a higher survival rate. Similarly, in a third meta-analysis published in 2017, aneurysm treatment within 48 h was compared to treatment between 48 h and 7 days, and to delayed (>7 days) treatment of poor-grade SAH patients. The meta-analysis included all published studies (even small case series) between 1990 and 2014 that reported on surgical or endovascular treatment for poor-grade SAH patients. A total of 26 studies with 1255 patients assessed outcomes by treatment timing. Based on these highly miscellaneous data, the authors concluded that poor-grade SAH patients treated within 48 h had the highest rates of good neurological outcome (61% compared to 40% for treatment between 48 h and 7 days, and 37% for delayed treatment). In another meta-analysis including also only poor-grade SAH patients (14 articles, 1111 patients), aneurysm treatment within < 24 h from symptom onset, clipping or coiling, was not associated with a decreased risk of poor functional outcome when compared to delayed (>24 h) treatment. A systematic review on 17 retrospective case series published before 2010 totalling 339 patients highlighted substantial variability across published case series. From 2015 to 2017, 232 patients received proximal balloon angioplasty, if needed followed by distal balloon angioplasty. Due to its practicability and favourable risk/benefit profile for aSAH patients, CTP measurement evolved as the most used perfusion imaging modality. CTP combines information about macro- and microvascular blood flow and may distinguish between reversible hypoperfusion and irreversible ischaemia. Quantitative image analyses with calculation of CBF, cerebral blood volume, mean transit time (MTT), time to peak and time to drain have been used to investigate impaired brain perfusion in aSAH patients. Increase in MTT has repeatedly been reported to accurately predict DCI before irreversible ischaemia occurs. In a prospective cohort of 64 aSAH patients with quantitative CTP at day 3, MTT predicted DCI with a sensitivity of 95% (95% CI, 83%–99%) and a negative predictive value of 96% (95% CI, 87%–99%) indicating very high diagnostic accuracy as screening tool for DCI. , In a meta-analysis of 570 patients, a decrease of CBF (pooled mean difference − 11.9 mL/100 g per minute [95% CI, −15.2 to −8.6]) and an increase in MTT (pooled mean difference 1.5 s [CI, 0.9–2.2]) during the high-risk phase (days 4–14 after ictus) was associated with DCI. However, absolute values of quantitative CTP parameters vary between different CT scanners and analysis algorithms. Therefore, measuring perfusion by CTP needs standardisation to define generalisable absolute perfusion thresholds after aSAH in future studies. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Although MRI is a sensitive modality for the early detection of cerebral ischaemia, its feasibility in the routine management of patients with aSAH during the high-risk period for DCI is limited by both patient-related and logistical factors. Many patients with aSAH are restless or have a decreased level of consciousness and therefore unable to lie still, which makes an MRI scan impossible. Furthermore, having a patient on the respiratory machine for about 20 min and monitoring that patient in the MR suite is challenging and often undesirable. In addition, when ischaemic lesions are detected on MRI, it is often difficult to determine whether these findings are attributable to DCI, acute ischaemic events (resulting from the acute aneurysm rupture) or procedure-related ischaemia. Collectively, these considerations limit the utility of MRI as a diagnostic tool in routine clinical practice. Emerging technologies, such as bedside ultra-low-field portable MRI systems and further reductions in acquisition time, may help to address some of these limitations in the future. Continuous EEG In unconscious patients, subtle neurological changes caused by focal cerebral ischaemia are often difficult to recognise. Continuous EEG (cEEG) may partially compensate for missing functional information. cEEG can be used for monitoring seizure activity and brain function in critically ill patients with altered mental status. In aSAH patients, seizure activity in cEEG has been reported in up to 19% of patients, which may contribute to worse clinical outcome. In addition to seizure detection, cEEG data can be analysed to define patterns of DCI-related pathological electric activity of the brain. For example, a decreased alpha to delta ratio is associated with DCI. In a prospective study of 227 consecutive aSAH patients, 103 were eligible for quantitative EEG analyses. In this cohort, cEEG predicted DCI with a sensitivity of 91% (95% CI, 81%–98%) and specificity of 83% (95% CI, 71%–93%) in low-risk patients, and a sensitivity of 95% (95% CI, 87%–99%) and specificity of 77% (95% CI, 36%–99%) in high-risk patients. However, the identified EEG patterns for DCI prediction and diagnosis need further validation in independent cohorts of aSAH patients with standardised definitions. In addition, clinical trials are needed to investigate whether therapeutic interventions based on cEEG findings decrease the risk of poor functional outcome in aSAH patients, to justify the high resource requirements for around-the-clock real-time data acquisition and interpretation. Invasive neuromonitoring probes Parenchymal monitoring probes can be used to obtain additional physiological data in neurologically unassessable aSAH patients, eg, ICP, regional CBF and the metabolic status of the brain. Intracranial pressure elevations are common and have been reported in up to 80% of poor grade aSAH patients. In unconscious patients with radiographic signs of hydrocephalus, ICP can be reliably monitored via an EVD (also see PICO 7). However, there is uncertainty about the risk/benefit profile of EVD insertion for ICP monitoring in aSAH patients without radiographic hydrocephalus. Parenchymal ICP probes are considered less invasive and commonly used for this indication. The SYNAPSE-ICU study was an international, prospective observational cohort study of 2395 patients with acute brain injury, of whom 521 (22%) had SAH, , which aimed to explore practice variation in ICP monitoring variation to prioritise uncertainties in the clinical management of critical care patients with acute brain injury and support further collaborative prospective studies. The study showed that SAH patients with ICP monitoring received more aggressive therapy treatments compared to patients without ICP monitoring. Intracranial pressure monitoring was associated with a reduction in poor functional outcome (OR: 0.14; 95% CI, 0.02–0.53) and case-fatality (HR: 0.25; 95% CI, 0.13–0.49) in SAH patients in a poor clinical condition, but not in those with 2 reactive pupils. Combined probes allow for continuous measurement of brain tissue oxygen pressure (PtbO 2 ) and ICP. This, in combination with systemic blood pressure measurements, may provide information about cerebral autoregulation. Brain tissue oxygen pressure monitoring has been reported to be sensitive in detection of metabolic cerebral compromise even in the absence of elevated ICP. In addition, microdialysis with quantification of interstitial metabolites, such as lactate and pyruvate, have been reported to detect metabolic derangements in situations without impaired PtbO 2 . Additional information EVD in acute hydrocephalus after aSAH The placement of an EVD in patients with acute hydrocephalus following aSAH, whether obstructive or communicating, is common practice in nearly all centres treating aSAH patients. External ventricular drain allows rapid control of acute hydrocephalus and ICP, and thereby is often considered a lifesaving treatment. In case of obstructive hydrocephalus or significant mass effect it is the only treatment possible, since LD or LP in these situations can lead to death by brain herniation. However, although commonly performed, EVD also has specific risks: brain haemorrhage along the catheter tract, catheter malposition, mechanical brain injury with putative long-term effect on motor function, cognition and risk of seizures, as well as catheter-related infection. , In addition, there is a debate regarding the indications for EVD placement, which can be clinical (decreased level of consciousness) and/or radiological (ventricular enlargement). Therefore, the risk/benefit ratio of EVD insertion must be weighed and alternatives considered. LD and LP in acute hydrocephalus after aSAH In case of acute and communicating hydrocephalus, a LD or LP can also be used instead of an EVD. Placement of an LD or performance of an LP probably carries a lower risk of complications than the placement of an EVD. However, CSF diversion by means of a LD or LP in case of obstructive hydrocephalus or significant cerebral oedema poses a risk of tonsillar herniation and thus death, and is therefore contraindicated in these situations. Regarding the LD, an observational study without control group reported no complications related to LD insertion (infection, brain herniation, over drainage) in 28 Fisher III aSAH patients. In another study, 229 Fisher III aSAH patients without obstructive hydrocephalus had an LD inserted, and the rate of CSF infection was 0.4%, which may be lower than that observed with EVD. One study in aSAH patients with symptomatic hydrocephalus retrospectively compared 56 patients with an EVD and 21 patients with a LD. The decision to treat with EVD or LD depended on the surgeon on call. Overall drain complications were 32.0% in patients with EVD and 9.5% in patients with LD. External ventricular drain vs LD complications consisted of haemorrhage (1.8% vs 0%), infection (7.1 vs 0%), clogged drain (25% vs 0%), dislodgement of drain (1.8% vs 4.6%) and replacement of drain (16% vs 4.8%). No case of cerebellar tonsillar herniation occurred. Regarding LP, in an observational study, 17 patients with symptomatic communicating hydrocephalus were treated by serial LPs. None had CSF infection or tonsillar herniation, and none required EVD insertion.
